MUJAHID:v2p760/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p760/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p760/r1.claim: Mujahid says a day of hardship is a day of hunger.

MUJAHID:v2p760/r2.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p760/r2.speaker: الحسن
MUJAHID:v2p760/r2.claim: Al-Hasan says it is a day when food is scarce or hard to find.

FARRA:v3p264/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p264/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p264/r1.claim: Arabic usually repeats lā across coordinated statements; here one lā covers the three parts of the steep path: freeing a slave or feeding during famine, then believing.

FARRA:v3p264/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p264/r2.speaker: العوام
FARRA:v3p264/r2.claim: The common reading coordinates the verbal noun “freeing a slave” with “feeding.”

FARRA:v3p264/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p264/r3.speaker: الحسن البصري وعلي بن أبي طالب
FARRA:v3p264/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib read the nouns as a coordinated pair, فك رقبة أو إطعام.

FARRA:v3p265/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p265/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p265/r1.claim: The reading فك رقبة أو إطعام best fits Arabic because إطعام is a noun and should coordinate with another noun; ثم كان also supports this parse.

FARRA:v3p265/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p265/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p265/r2.claim: The alternative reading is also possible if an omitted أن is supplied; a poem with أن in the second clause shows that it can be understood in the first.

FARRA:v3p265/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p265/r3.speaker: شاعر
FARRA:v3p265/r3.claim: An unnamed poet uses overt أن in the second coordinated clause, illustrating the elided أن in the earlier clause.

FARRA:v3p265/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p265/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p265/r4.claim: Masghaba means famine; alternatively, if dhī masghaba modifies the orphan, it describes feeding an orphan during famine.

MAJAZ:v2p299/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p299/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p299/r5.claim: The obstacle is freeing a slave or feeding someone on a day of famine.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#8/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#8/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p528#8/r1.claim: Masghaba means famine; saghab is hunger and sāghib a hungry person, with several verbal forms for becoming hungry.

TUSTARI:90:14/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:90:14/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:90:14/r1.claim: Feeding in a day of hunger is necessary sustenance for faith, not an indulgence in the injustice and excess of natural appetite.

TAB-FULL:v24p426/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p426/r1.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v24p426/r1.claim: A day of masghabah is a day of famine or hunger.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses a day of masghaba as a famine.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r2.speaker: إبراهيم
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3435/r2.claim: Ibrahim says it is a day when food is scarce.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r11.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r11.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p229/r11.claim: The steep path means freeing a slave or feeding someone on a day of hunger; Abū Hurayra reports that freeing a slave earns release from the Fire for each limb.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r12.speaker: الحسن
NAHHAS:v5p229/r12.claim: With Abū Rajāʾ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Kathīr, and al-Kisāʾī, he reads the words as verbal commands or past verbs: freeing a slave or feeding on a hungry day.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r13.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p229/r13.claim: He prefers the verbal reading because ثم كان is a past verb and should coordinate with another past verb.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r14.speaker: الأخفش
NAHHAS:v5p229/r14.claim: Al-Akhfash, Abū Ḥātim, and Abū ʿUbayd prefer the nominal reading.

NAHHAS:v5p229/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p229/r15.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p229/r15.claim: Both are sound readings and one may not attack the reading transmitted by the community; the past-verb coordination argument fails because it cannot coordinate by sense as proposed.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r1.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p232/r1.claim: He allows the alternate reading by supplying an implied an and cites a poem; the author says the reading would then require an accusative and that an cannot be omitted without a substitute.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r2.speaker: أبو عبيد
NAHHAS:v5p232/r2.claim: He says the nominal ‘freeing a slave’ is the choice because it explains what the obstacle is.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r3.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
NAHHAS:v5p232/r3.claim: He claims that every verse asking ‘what will make you know’ supplies an explanation, while ‘what makes you know’ does not.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p232/r4.claim: He rejects Sufyān's rule: the Qurʾān explains both the Calamity and the Reality after asking what they are.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r5.speaker: الحسن
NAHHAS:v5p232/r5.claim: With Abū Rajāʾ, he reads dhā as the object fed and an adjective of the orphan.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r6.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v5p232/r6.claim: He analyzes dhā masghaba as an adjective before the orphan, despite the adjective preceding its noun.

NAHHAS:v5p232/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p232/r7.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p232/r7.claim: He calls that analysis an obvious error because an adjective cannot precede its noun; dhā masghaba is governed by feed and the orphan is an apposition.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r2.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r2.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r2.claim: With nominative endings, فك and إطعام are verbal nouns; with fatḥa they are past-tense verbs whose subject is the previously mentioned person, with رقبة and orphan accusatives.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r3.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r3.speaker: author
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r3.claim: On the verbal-noun reading, crossing the steep path means freeing a captive or feeding an orphan during famine, conditioned on faith.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r4.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r4.speaker: البصريون
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r4.claim: Basran grammarians say a verbal noun with tanwīn or the definite article governs a noun like a verb because the noun is the verb's source.

IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r5.author: Ibn Khālawayh (attr.)
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r5.speaker: الكوفيون
IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p371/r5.claim: Kufans deny that an inflected or definite verbal noun governs nouns; they derive the accusative orphan from an implied verb and coordinate مسكينا with يتيما.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r1.claim: These readers use the verbal forms فك رقبة or أطعم, with رقبة in the accusative; Abū ʿAmr's transmitters report minor differences over the two forms and their attachment.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r2.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر ونافع وحمزة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r2.claim: These readers use the verbal noun إطعام alongside فك رقبة.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r5.claim: Abū ʿUbaydah says the person failed to cross the path in worldly life, then takes freeing a captive or feeding as its explanation.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r6.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r6.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p413/r6.claim: With the verbal-noun reading, an omitted اقتحام is required: otherwise the sentence equates the path itself with the event of freeing a captive, unlike the intended explanatory relation.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r3.speaker: أبو الحسن
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r3.claim: Abū al-Ḥasan calls one of the two readings better and says it is the one he reads; he also allows describing a day as hungry, as one describes a night as sleeping.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r4.speaker: author
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p414/r4.claim: The verbal reading may explain the challenge through its actions; an explanatory clause need not copy the nominal-predicate construction in other examples, and meaning can link the clauses.

SULAMI:v2p396#2/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p396#2/r1.speaker: المغربي
SULAMI:v2p396#2/r1.claim: One fasts for ten days, then gives away food when it comes, preferring the hungry self to the needy person who receives it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p279/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p279/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p279/r3.claim: A day of severe hunger is a famine caused by drought or high prices.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r1.speaker: أبو عبيدة وابن عباس ومجاهد وعكرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r1.claim: Masghaba means hunger or famine; sاغib and saghbān describe a hungry person.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r2.speaker: الحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r2.claim: He describes the day as one when food is eagerly sought.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r3.speaker: أبو علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p29/r3.claim: A day can be described as hungry, just as a night can be called sleeping and a day fasting.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:14-20/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:14-20/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:90:14-20/r1.claim: A day of severe hunger is a famine.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r2.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, and al-Kisai read فك as a verb with ‘a neck’ as its object and ‘or he fed’ as a past verb; others read a noun phrase, ‘freeing a neck or feeding.’

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r5.speaker: البراء بن عازب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p432/r5.claim: The Prophet distinguishes freeing a person outright from contributing to the purchase price; he also recommends a productive gift, helping a needy relative, feeding the hungry, giving water, enjoining right, and guarding one’s tongue if unable.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p433/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p433/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p433/r2.claim: A day of مسغبة is famine; سغب means to be hungry.

KASHSHAF:90:14/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:14/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:90:14/r1.claim: Masghabah derives from hunger, maqrabah from kinship, and matrabah from poverty and being stuck to the earth; atraba means becoming rich, like athra.

KASHSHAF:90:14/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:14/r2.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:90:14/r2.claim: The Prophet explains a person of matrabah as someone whose home is a rubbish dump.

KASHSHAF:90:14/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:14/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:90:14/r3.claim: Describing a day as possessing hunger follows the grammatical pattern of saying that someone is 'possessed of toil.'

KASHSHAF:90:14/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:90:14/r4.speaker: الحسن
KASHSHAF:90:14/r4.claim: Al-Hasan reads the phrase with accusative dhā masghabah, governed by feeding, meaning food on a hunger-stricken day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r7.claim: Masghaba is famine; a saghib is hungry, and the word may mean general famine or an individual's hunger.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r8.speaker: جمهور الناس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r8.claim: Most readers use dhi as an adjective agreeing with the day.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r9.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وأبو رجاء
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p485#2/r9.claim: These readers use accusative dha, governed by atʿama or itʿam; the omitted noun is a person experiencing famine.

TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r3.claim: Masghabah is hunger; feeding on a famine day is praised.

TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r4.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r4.claim: A Prophetic report promises entry through a special gate of Paradise to whoever feeds a hungry person on a day of famine.

TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r5.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r5.claim: A Prophetic report names feeding a starving Muslim as one of the causes of forgiveness.

TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r6.speaker: محمد بن عمر بن يزيد
TABRISI:90:1-20#7/r6.claim: Al-Rida advised repeatedly donating a handful of food for the inquirer's seriously ill son, citing the call to approach the obstacle.

TABRISI:90:1-20/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:90:1-20/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:90:1-20/r12.claim: Masghabah means famine; sāghib describes someone hungry.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r1.speaker: قراءة أوأطعم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r1.claim: One reading has aṭʿama with fatḥa on the hamza and mīm and a still ṭāʾ, without alif.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p135#2/r5.claim: Masghaba means famine; the verb saghiba means to become hungry.

RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r1.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari derives masghaba from hunger, maqraba from kinship or closeness, and matraba from becoming poor and stuck to earth; atraba means becoming wealthy like earth in abundance.

RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r2.speaker: الواحدي
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r2.claim: Al-Wahidi calls matraba a verbal noun meaning becoming so poor one clings to the dust.

RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r3.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r3.claim: Al-Hasan explains a day of hunger as a day on which people are eager for food; Arabic similarly calls a night 'sleeping' or a day 'fasting.'

RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r4.claim: Spending during famine and necessity is harder for the soul and earns greater reward, as in 2:177 and 76:8.

RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r5.speaker: الحسن
RAZI-FULL:v31p168#4/r5.claim: Al-Hasan reads dhā masghaba in the accusative as an adjective of the day: feeding on a day characterized by hunger.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r1.claim: Masghabah means famine, and saghib means hungry.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r2.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r2.claim: He reads dhā with an alif in dhā masghabah; Abu Ubayda cites a poem about a hungry neighbor as evidence.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r3.claim: Feeding is virtuous, especially during famine when food is scarce.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r4.speaker: النخعي
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r4.claim: He says it means a day when food is hard to find.

QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r5.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:90:14-15/r5.claim: A Prophetic report says feeding a hungry Muslim is one of the acts that bring mercy.

BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r3.claim: The pass is freeing a captive or feeding, during famine, a related orphan or impoverished person; repeated negation fits the multiple acts, and the terms mean hunger, kinship, and poverty.

BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:90:10-16/r4.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and al-Kisāʾī read فك رقبة أو أطعم as a substitute for اقتحم.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#9/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#9/r12.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p340#9/r12.claim: Describing the day as possessing famine follows the idiom calling people 'possessors of toil,' meaning afflicted with toil.

QASHANI:90:8-14/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:90:8-14/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:90:8-14/r4.claim: Feeding the needy exemplifies generosity and chastity; faith is wisdom, patience is courage that depends on certainty, and compassion is justice, completing the four cardinal virtues.

QASHANI:90:8-14/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:90:8-14/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:90:8-14/r5.claim: The order begins with chastity and generosity, then the higher wisdom of faith, then patience which requires certainty, and ends with compassion as justice; each named quality stands for its broader virtue.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p478/r5.claim: Saghab is widespread hunger; a person is said to saghiba when hungry.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p408/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p408/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p408/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah explain a day of مسغبة as a day of famine or hunger; Ibrahim says food is scarce, and Qatadah says it is especially desired.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r6.claim: Feeding on a day of severe hunger means general famine in a hungry place and time; it requires resisting stinginess and fear by trusting God.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r7.claim: The paired descriptions use interlocking omission: the orphan is near kin, while the dust-covered poor person is in extreme need; together they imply their opposites and include strangers by stronger reason.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p432/r8.claim: The orphan’s kinship evokes compassion and the poor person’s dust evokes tenderness; feeding aims only to meet need, and distant orphans and unrelated poor people are included a fortiori.

DURR-FULL:v8p524/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r7.speaker: إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r7.claim: He described it as a day when food is scarce.

DURR-FULL:v8p524/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r8.speaker: الحسن وأبو رجاء العطاردي
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r8.claim: They recited the phrase with ذا مسغبة instead of ذي مسغبة.

DURR-FULL:v8p524/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r9.speaker: جابر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v8p524/r9.claim: The Prophet said feeding a hungry Muslim is among the acts that bring forgiveness; al-Hakim authenticated the report.

DURR-FULL:v8p525/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p525/r10.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v8p525/r10.claim: He said that, after obligatory duties, no deed is dearer to God than feeding a poor person.

BURSEVI:v10p339/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p339/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p339/r1.claim: A day of masghaba is a day of famine caused by drought or high prices; al-Raghib defines it as hunger with fatigue, and sometimes thirst with fatigue.

BURSEVI:v10p339/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p339/r10.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p339/r10.claim: Emancipation and feeding are singled out because they are difficult: people readily spend on desires and surplus buildings but begrudge even a small gift or bite to an orphan or poor person whom they disdain.

BURSEVI:v10p339/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p339/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p339/r2.claim: Feeding is specified for a famine day because giving wealth then weighs more heavily on the self and earns greater reward.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r1.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r1.claim: Abu Hayyan says masghaba means widespread hunger, though saghiba can also describe an individual becoming hungry.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r2.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r2.claim: Al-Raghib defines masghaba as hunger accompanied by fatigue, and says it can also describe thirst with fatigue.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas explains the verse's masghaba simply as hunger, without qualification.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r4.speaker: إبراهيم
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r4.claim: Ibrahim says it is a day when food is scarce; Alusi notes that this describes the circumstance rather than the word's lexical meaning.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p138/r5.claim: Describing a day as possessing hunger is like saying a person is possessed of toil, a night of sleep, or a day of fasting.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r1.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir and the two grammarian-readers use past verbs fakka and atʿama with raqabatan in the accusative; on this reading fakk is an appositive of iqtahama, with intervening words parenthetical.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r2.speaker: أبو رجاء
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r2.claim: Abu Rajaʾ also reads dhā masghaba with the alif, making a person in need the object of feeding; he and al-Hasan have a related accusative reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r3.speaker: بعض التابعين
ALUSI-FULL:v30p139/r3.claim: Some Successors read fakk raqabatin in construct and atʿama as a past verb, coordinated with the verbal noun by interpreting it verbally.

ELMALILI:90:12-20/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r10.claim: Feeding people during a widespread famine can save lives and is therefore a major act of courage like freeing a slave.

ELMALILI:90:12-20/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r13.claim: Feeding a near orphan or destitute person during general famine requires heart and effort; the boastful person with abundant wealth did not undertake this ascent.

ELMALILI:90:12-20/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r8.claim: Mesghaba is a verbal noun for hunger, especially hunger amid hardship and fatigue; Abu Hayyan says it can also refer to thirst.

ELMALILI:90:12-20/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r9.speaker: Ebû Hayyân
ELMALILI:90:12-20/r9.claim: Abu Hayyan says mesghaba means widespread famine; its generality follows from dhi, which describes a day characterized by hunger, rather than merely a day of hunger.

QUTB-ZILAL:90:14/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:90:14/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:90:14/r1.claim: Masghabah means famine; feeding on a day when food is scarce tests the reality of a person’s faith.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r4.claim: Alternatively, the phrase is a rebuking question with its interrogative particle omitted: the boaster wasted wealth on gambling and wine, so why did he not spend generously on liberation and feeding during famine?

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p355/r5.claim: The single لا can negate the past without repetition because اقتحم entails the later acts of freeing and feeding, or because the later faith clause supplies the second negation; anything that prevents ambiguity can serve similarly, as an example from al-Ḥarīrī shows.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r3.speaker: نافع وابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة وأبو جعفر ويعقوب وخلف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r3.claim: These readers pronounce فك and إطعام in the nominative; the clause explains the العقبة as freeing a person or feeding, with an omitted predicate, and the hard deed metaphor needs no added implied noun.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r4.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p357/r4.claim: They read فك as an active past verb with رقبة as its object and اطعم as another past verb; this explains the preceding negation or substitutes for اقتحم العقبة.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r3.claim: مسغبة means hunger and is a mafaʿala verbal noun from سغب; a day marked by hunger means a period of famine, especially cold or drought, rather than one ordinary day.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r4.claim: Feeding during famine is especially meritorious because people hoard food against prolonged scarcity, making such generosity the difficult pass and other good deeds lesser steps.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r5.claim: يتيما is the direct object of the verbal noun إطعام; governing an object with an indefinite unmodified verbal noun is the stronger grammatical analysis, though Kufans reject it and posit an omitted verb.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p358/r6.claim: An orphan is a fatherless child before puberty; weak work, lack of a provider, and shyness in asking make the child especially vulnerable, while ذا مقربة adds kinship merit. A مسكين is poor, and ذا متربة marks conventionally severe need.

BINTSHATI:v1p185/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p185/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p185/r4.claim: The author rejects the need for allegorical explanations because the Qur’an itself answers its question by defining the obstacle through emancipation, feeding, faith, patience, and mercy.

BINTSHATI:v1p186/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r3.claim: The author portrays Meccan injustice as desecrating the Prophet’s sanctuary while powerful owners enslave people and leave relatives and the poor hungry.

BINTSHATI:v1p186/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p186/r4.claim: The surah calls people to struggle against slavery, class divisions, and social oppression by appealing to their innate capacity for moral effort.

BINTSHATI:v1p187/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p187/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p187/r1.claim: Masghabah is famine or widespread hunger; depicting a day of famine heightens the horror of a needy neighbor going unfed, as Abū Ḥayyān also says.

BINTSHATI:v1p188/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p188/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p188/r1.claim: The author takes thumma as real sequence: restoring dignity through emancipation and social justice through feeding are prerequisites for faith and its mutual exhortations.

BINTSHATI:v1p188/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p188/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p188/r4.claim: The author rejects readings that detach faith from emancipation and feeding, arguing genuine faith requires resistance to tyranny, enslavement, and indifference to the poor.

BINTSHATI:v1p189/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v1p189/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v1p189/r1.claim: The order makes human dignity and social justice grounds of faith; a society that accepts human enslavement and starvation cannot sustain sincere faith.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:1-4:kommentar/r3.claim: The verse presents Mecca as a place of ordinary social life as well as ritual, dependent on support for vulnerable people; religious norms therefore extend beyond worship.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r3.claim: After a negative example, the text calls for wealth to be used to care for vulnerable people rather than for self-aggrandizement, imitating God's care for humanity.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r4.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r4.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r4.claim: The virtue list adapts Isaiah 58:5–7 in a different context: Isaiah critiques merely external ritual, whereas the Qur'an grounds moral duty in God's grace to all humanity.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r5.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r5.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r5.claim: The biblical allusion overwrites the heroic worldview carried by the poetry cited in verse 6, making scripture an ally against the values of canonical pre-Islamic verse.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r6.speaker: Neuwirth
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r6.claim: Neuwirth notes that masġaba is an ordinary word, while the orphan and poor are described with poetic analogical forms ḏū maqraba and ḏū matraba.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r7.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r7.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:11-16:kommentar/r7.claim: The biblically inspired but deliberately Arabized virtue list culminates the sura and spells out the normative consequences of creation and God's care.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r1.claim: The catalogue of virtues has biblical roots and belongs to the prophetic call to support orphans and the poor, with parallels noted at 107:2–3.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r2.claim: The catalogue clearly echoes Isaiah 58:6–7: freeing slaves, feeding the hungry, housing the poor, clothing the naked, and helping kin.

CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r3.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:90:13-16:anmerkung/r3.claim: Both the Qur'anic and Isaiah catalogues begin with freeing slaves and then identify poor people and relatives as recipients of aid, though their framing questions differ.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r2.claim: Feeding the poor has the broader sense of meeting all their needs, and its merit rises during famine.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p326/r3.claim: The famine qualifier strengthens the appeal because feeding the poor is especially valuable in famine conditions.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r4.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r4.claim: The era's gravest human problems were slavery, poverty, and lack of mercy; remedies were freeing slaves, feeding orphans and the poor, and urging patience and compassion.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r5.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:90:8/r5.claim: This summary of Islamic social ethics gives examples rather than an exhaustive or restrictive list of good works.

QIRAAT-ER:90:14:2#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:90:14:2#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:90:14:2#1/r1.claim: The variant changes the verbal noun feeding into a Form IV perfect verb, a completed act of feeding.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r1.claim: Al-Balad names the orphan and poor also mentioned in al-Fajr, answering the earlier charge that people fail to honor orphans or urge feeding the poor.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r2.claim: Since al-Fajr condemns intense love of wealth and devouring inheritance, al-Balad says overcoming the obstacle requires sharing wealth with others.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r3.claim: The relation between eating inheritance and feeding during famine is direct: just as people eat, they should feed others.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r4.speaker: أبو حيان
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r4.claim: Abu Hayyan says al-Balad follows al-Fajr's discussion of testing people through ease and hardship, their blameworthy traits, and the fates of people and believers.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r5.speaker: الألوسي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p242/r5.claim: Al-Alusi says the passage answers condemnation of loving wealth, consuming inheritance, and neglecting the poor by naming what wealth holders should do: free captives and feed people during famine.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r1.speaker: الألوسي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r1.claim: Al-Alusi adds that freeing captives and feeding during famine are virtues expected of a wealthy person, just as the previous surah mentioned the contented soul and this one describes what brings contentment.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p243/r2.claim: Al-Balad comprehensively presents the elements of a message: Mecca, its resident Messenger, humanity as recipients, faith and good works as the message, and believers and disbelievers as the two response groups.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p253/r2.claim: The parent feeding a child connects the oath to feeding the hungry during famine; hardship, patience, and mercy govern the surah and childcare alike.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p256/r4.claim: The parent-and-child oath also anticipates the difficult ascent and the hardships of hunger experienced by the orphan and poor person.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p266/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p266/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p266/r1.claim: Iqtiham conveys danger and difficulty better than merely traversing; the rough ascent and care for the hungry, orphan, and poor suit kabad as hardship and strength.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r2.claim: Masghabah means widespread famine rather than an individual's hunger; feeding during general scarcity, when food is scarce and hoarded, is a particularly difficult social ascent.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p271/r3.claim: Feeding when supplies are plentiful differs from feeding amid scarcity, fear of loss, and reluctance to sell; the latter truly climbs a hard social obstacle.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r1.claim: Aw marks alternatives rather than requiring all duties together: feeding either needy class, separately or in combination, suffices for the intended variety.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r3.claim: The enslaved, hungry, orphaned, and destitute are among those who endure the greatest toil; liberating and feeding them enact mercy, while they need patience.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p272/r4.claim: The man who boasts of wasting much money spent it in the wrong place, since he neither fed a hungry person nor freed anyone.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p274/r1.claim: The surah's hardships call for patience: choosing either path, climbing the ascent, serving the enslaved, enduring famine, and caring for orphans and the destitute all demand perseverance.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p275/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p275/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p275/r1.claim: Famine is a crucial time to spread mercy, and orphans and poor people are among those most in need of it; believers should enjoin mercy on one another.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p278/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p278/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT:p278/r1.claim: The words for famine, kinship, destitution, mercy, and the right and left groups share the pattern maf'alah, matching action, description, and reward.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p386/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p386/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p386/r1.claim: Al-Balad's command to feed answers al-Fajr's condemnation of consuming inheritance greedily: as people eat, they should also feed others.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p399/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p399/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p399/r4.claim: Masghabah denotes collective rather than individual hunger, unlike saghab; the passage begins explaining why this word suits the verse.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r1.claim: Masghabah also conveys hunger with exhaustion, unlike hunger in general; makhmaṣah specifically entails a shrunken abdomen, so the word portrays a severe communal famine when food is scarce.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r2.claim: Ṭaʿām can mean either the act of eating or the food itself; commentators recognize both senses elsewhere, but this famine context calls for feeding the hungry.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p400/r3.claim: The verbal noun iṭʿām is used instead of “that you feed” because the present famine requires immediate feeding, while the latter construction would point to future action.

STUDYQURAN:90:14/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:90:14/r1.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:90:14/r1.claim: Giving wealth is harder in times of need but more beneficial; al-Rāzī glosses the verse with the teaching of 2:177 and 76:8.
